title: Same lake, two radars
caption_simple: Radar sees through cloud and at night. Calm water looks dark because it bounces the radar signal away, so the lake stands out from the brighter land around it.
caption_expert: γ0 backscatter, boxcar 5×5, 10 m lake-chip grid (UTM 32N), −25…0 dB. Left: Sentinel-1 C-band VV, 17 Jun 2026 17:20 UTC (orbit 88); right: NISAR L-band HH GCOV, 19 Jun 2026 18:12 UTC (D80/F70). Cross-sensor pair (different band, polarisation, incidence): illustrates the signal, not evidence of change.
source: ESA Copernicus Sentinel-1 RTC (Microsoft Planetary Computer); NASA/JPL–ISRO NISAR GCOV (ASF DAAC)

title: Step 1 · Where is the lake?
caption_simple: We first map the lake as it was before the failure: the pixels that were water in most Sentinel-1 images. Every later measurement is counted inside this outline only.
caption_expert: Water frequency over 19 pre-failure Sentinel-1 RTC VV images (2026-05-16 → 2026-06-16), each thresholded by Otsu (clamped −23…−13.5 dB). Polygon = frequency ≥ 50 %, component nearest the dam, holes filled, dilated 100 m: 4.68 km² on the 10 m grid.
source: ESA Copernicus Sentinel-1 RTC (Microsoft Planetary Computer); this project (02_reservoir.py)

title: Step 2 · A threshold for each image
caption_simple: Wind and wet mud change how dark water looks. Instead of one fixed cut-off, each image gets its own, found where its 'water' and 'land' pixels separate best.
caption_expert: Otsu threshold on γ0 dB (boxcar 5×5) in the lake polygon + 300 m land ring, clamped −23…−13.5 dB. Sentinel-1 VV 17 Jun 2026 (o88): T = −13.5 dB (at the clamp limit) → 2.92 km² (1.91–3.27 for T ±2 dB); a fixed −18 dB gives 0.10 km² because the wind-roughened lake sits at about −15…−17 dB. Threshold ±2 dB moves areas by a median ±23 % (validation A1).
source: ESA Copernicus Sentinel-1 RTC (Microsoft Planetary Computer); this project (02_reservoir.py)

title: Step 3 · One mask per image
caption_simple: The same method is applied to every image. The lake shrinks over the weeks after the failure and starts to recover with the autumn rain.
caption_expert: Adaptive-Otsu water masks inside the lake polygon, 10 m grid. Areas (km², raw per track): S1 10 Jun o161 2.79, S1 17 Jun o88 2.92, NISAR D80 19 Jun 2.49, 1 Jul 2.50, 13 Jul 2.05, 29 Oct 1.67. S1 → NISAR is cross-sensor (C vs L band); compare within one sensor and track.
source: ESA Copernicus Sentinel-1 RTC (Microsoft Planetary Computer); NASA/JPL–ISRO NISAR GCOV (ASF DAAC)

title: Step 4 · The lake area over time
caption_simple: After the gate failed the lake shrank over several weeks, not overnight, until the gate was repaired in mid-July. It stayed low in summer and rose again with the autumn rain.
caption_expert: 133 water-area measurements (131 good, 2 low-confidence) from NISAR GCOV HH (D80, A101, A173, D8) and Sentinel-1 RTC VV (o88, o161, o168), adaptive Otsu inside the lake polygon, harmonised per track on Aug–Oct medians; bars = threshold ±2 dB. NISAR gap 2026-07-27 → 2026-08-13. Event dates are press reports (REPORTED). Right after the failure, L-band reads wet mud as water, so NISAR area lags.
source: ESA Copernicus Sentinel-1 RTC; NASA/JPL–ISRO NISAR GCOV (ASF DAAC); events: Tunisian press (REPORTED)

title: Step 5 · When does a drop become an alert?
caption_simple: NISAR and Sentinel-1 together would have raised an alarm on 22 June, five days after the failure, with no ground sensor. Red points are confirmed alerts, yellow ones confirmed warnings.
caption_expert: Harmonised area vs median of all passes in the previous 21 days; WARNING < −12 %, ALERT < −20 %, each confirmed by an independent pass within 6 days. First ALERT 2026-06-22: S1 o161 −20.5 %, confirmed by S1 o88 −28.8 %; 0 flags before the failure. NISAR is in the baseline; first NISAR flag 26 Jun (A173, WARNING). Oct–Nov flags follow a real multi-sensor decline and need an operator check.
source: Rule-based detector (this project, 03_anomaly.py) on MEASURED NISAR + Sentinel-1 areas

title: Step 6 · How far did the water drop?
caption_simple: The SWOT satellite measured the lake surface 3.75 m lower on 28 June than on 7 June. Multiplying by the lake area gives a storage loss of about 13 million m³.
caption_expert: SWOT Hydrocron LakeSP, PLD lake 1530007983; quality_f 0 vs 1, ± wse_u. 260.54 → 256.79 ± 0.08 m (2026-06-07 → 2026-06-28, Δh −3.75 m). ΔV = trapezoid ∫A·dh = −12.7 Mm³ (−17.1…−7.8; radar vs SWOT area), MODELLED net storage change, not the release. 2 passes from 2024 not shown.
source: SWOT (NASA/CNES) Hydrocron LakeSP; ΔV: this project (07_level_volume.py), MODELLED

title: Step 7 · Where does the water go?
caption_simple: Water runs downhill. Following the slope cell by cell from the dam traces the 101 km path the released water takes, past Jendouba to the Sidi Salem reservoir.
caption_expert: D8 steepest descent (pysheds) on GEM-15 (experimental) DTM 15 m block-averaged to 30 m, HydroRIVERS main stem burned −2 m, depressions filled. Path 101.0 km; Jendouba km 37.6 (town 4.4 km off the path), Medjerda confluence km 44.9, Bou Salem km 66.8. Test D2: 98.8 % of the path within 300 m of OSM rivers.
source: GEM-15 DTM produced by Google (CC-BY 4.0) (doi:10.31223/X55N75); HydroRIVERS v1.0; OpenStreetMap; this project (04_routing_hand.py)

title: Step 8 · Fill the valley like a bathtub
caption_simple: A quick first estimate: spread the released water at one height along the whole valley. 21 million m³ reaches about 1.0 m above the river and covers about 26 km². It ignores timing, so it is a screening map, not a forecast.
caption_expert: HAND = height above the main-stem flow-path cell each cell drains to (D8, GEM-15 30 m), corridor ≤ 5 km, dam → Sidi Salem, reservoirs excluded. V(h) = Σ(h − HAND)·900 m². 21 Mm³ → h 0.97 m, 26.4 km² (map: 26.5 km²). Static bathtub: no timing or attenuation; HAND ≈ 0 in filled channel reaches makes small volumes wide and shallow.
source: GEM-15 DTM produced by Google (CC-BY 4.0); HydroRIVERS v1.0; this project (04_routing_hand.py)

title: Step 9 · Let the water flow (2D model)
caption_simple: A flood model lets the water move over the terrain hour by hour. For the June 2026 volume it shows where the water could spread and roughly when it reaches the Medjerda (13–19 hours). These are scenarios, not forecasts.
caption_expert: ANUGA 4.2.0 (DE0), 69,616 triangles ≤ 2,500 m², GEM-15 30 m with flow path lowered 2 m, Manning n from WorldCover, triangular 12 h release at the dam, 48 h simulated, wet > 0.1 m. Wet 21/50/195 Mm³: 19.3 / 35.4 / 71.8 km²; confluence arrival 12.9 / 9.3 / 6.2 h. Mesh-sensitive (test E4): report arrival as 13–19 h. 195 Mm³ is hypothetical. No bathymetry, no calibration.
source: ANUGA (Geoscience Australia / ANU); GEM-15 DTM produced by Google (CC-BY 4.0); ESA WorldCover 2021; this project (05_anuga_scenarios.py)

title: Step 10 · What lies in the water's way?
caption_simple: We count the fields, buildings, roads and people inside each flood footprint. This is exposure, not damage, and the two models cover different stretches of the valley.
caption_expert: HAND values interpolated from flood/hand_lut.json at V (whole 101 km corridor, static); ANUGA from impacts/impacts.json (Reach 1 only, max depth > 0.1 m). 21 Mm³: cropland HAND 1,308 ha vs ANUGA 1,112 ha. Population is not computed for ANUGA. OSM buildings/roads are incomplete (lower bounds); WorldPop is itself a model.
source: ESA WorldCover 2021; OpenStreetMap contributors; WorldPop 2020; this project (04, 06)

title: V2 preview · Rivers found from terrain alone
caption_simple: V2 preview: from a terrain model alone, the computer finds the rivers, the path the water would take below a dam and the corridor to check for flooding.
caption_expert: V2 preview. D8 flow accumulation (pysheds) on GEM-15 30 m: cells with contributing area ≥ 10 km² (colour = log area); main-stem path 101.0 km dam → Sidi Salem; HAND corridor ≤ 5 km. Computed for Mellègue only; generalisation to other dams is roadmap work.
source: GEM-15 DTM produced by Google (CC-BY 4.0); HydroRIVERS v1.0; this project (04_routing_hand.py)

title: V2 preview · Any dam, its catchment, automatically
caption_simple: V2 preview: for any dam, find all the land whose rain flows into it. The Mellègue dam collects water from 10,315 km², much of it across the border in Algeria.
caption_expert: V2 preview. Each catchment = union of HydroBASINS level-12 sub-basins upstream of the HydroRIVERS main-stem reach nearest the dam point: Mellègue 10,314.9 km², Sidi Salem 18,069.4 km² (00_context_data.py), drawn over HydroBASINS level 6. Dam points from OpenStreetMap; flow path from GEM-15 D8.

title: V2 preview · Watching a site upstream
caption_simple: V2 preview: satellites can also keep an eye on changes upstream. This box marks a possible construction site for the planned Upper Mellègue dam. It is unconfirmed.
caption_expert: V2 preview. Sentinel-2 L2A true colour (B4/B3/B2, 10 m, common 1–99.3 % stretch), 7 Apr vs 13 Nov 2026, tile T32SME/SMF. Box 8.62–8.63 E, 36.24–36.25 N flagged by visual inspection only; no detection algorithm, no official confirmation.
source: ESA Copernicus Sentinel-2 L2A (Microsoft Planetary Computer); visual inspection (this project)

title: V2 preview · How often NISAR looks at Tunisia
caption_simple: V2 preview: NISAR delivered 1,754 products over Tunisia in its first months, and imaged the Mellègue dam on 31 different dates.
caption_expert: V2 preview. ASF catalogue search over Tunisia: 1,754 unique NISAR products (L1 RSLC, L2 GSLC/GCOV/GUNW, L3 SME2) 2026-06-17 → 2026-10-31 (GCOV 390, GSLC 392, GUNW 217, RSLC 396, SME2 359); GCOV over the Mellègue dam on 31 dates (A101/20, A173/20, D8/70, D80/70); longest gap 2026-07-27 → 2026-08-13.
source: NASA/JPL–ISRO NISAR product catalogue (ASF DAAC search, TESTS/nisar_tunisia_output)
